extraction.name: SWE-Gym
extraction.description: The first environment for training software engineering agents. SWE-Gym contains 2,438 real-world task instances, each comprising a Python codebase with an executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language. It is constructed from real-world GitHub issues and pull requests in 11 popular Python repositories, with pre-configured executable environments and expert-validated test cases. The paper also describes SWE-Gym Lite with 230 easier tasks and SWE-Gym Raw with 64,689 Python GitHub issues without executable environments.
extraction.creator: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang
extraction.citeAs: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang. Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym. Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: SWE-Gym was constructed from real-world software engineering tasks sourced from pull requests and GitHub issues in Python repositories. The authors first used SEART GitHub search to filter repositories created before July 1, 2022 with more than 500 stars, at least 300 lines of code, more than 500 pull requests, and 100 contributors, resulting in 358 repositories. They then used SWE-Bench's instance extraction script to convert repositories into task instances containing the issue description, repository snapshot, and unit tests, yielding 64,689 raw instances. They focused on 11 repositories with numerous instances and semi-manually created executable environments for them. They generalized SWE-Bench's versioning script to collect version numbers for each instance and manually configured dependencies for each task instance using repository configuration files, CI scripts, or documentation. They then used SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure the gold patch passed more unit tests than the original code, and after validation and filtering out failed instances obtained 2,438 unit-test-validated instances. The process required approximately 200 human annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Software Collection, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data source consists of Python GitHub repositories, GitHub issues, pull requests, repository snapshots, unit tests, and human-submitted gold patches. SWE-Gym Raw contains 64,689 Python GitHub issues spanning 358 Python repositories without executable environments. The final SWE-Gym dataset uses tasks from 11 popular open-source Python repositories.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Repositories were selected if created before July 1, 2022.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors associated instances with version numbers, generalized SWE-Bench's versioning script to support versioning via script execution, semi-automatically collected versions for each instance based on repository information such as pyproject.toml and git tags, manually configured dependencies for each task instance, and filtered out failed instances after execution-based validation.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Each repository was converted into task instances using SWE-Bench's instance extraction script. For the final dataset, the authors semi-manually created executable environments for 11 repositories, configured dependencies using requirements files, CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at issue creation time, and validated each instance with SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure the gold patch passed more unit tests than the original code. Failed instances were filtered out. For SWE-Gym Lite, they followed the SWE-Bench Lite filtering pipeline and excluded tasks requiring editing more than one file, tasks with poorly described problem statements, tasks with excessively complex ground-truth code diffs, and tests focused on error message validation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The paper states that annotations were done by a subset of the authors during the process of manually configuring dependencies and creating executable environments for task instances. This semi-manual process used relevant configuration files, CI scripts, or documentation from repository snapshots to set up environments, followed by execution-based validation to verify that the human-submitted gold patch passed more unit tests than the original code. The paper also describes verifier labels for agent trajectories as successful or unsuccessful based on whether unit tests indicated the problem was solved.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors used execution-based validation to ensure that the gold patch passed more unit tests than the original code, and filtered out failed instances. For verifier training, trajectories were labeled as successful or unsuccessful, and the paper reports that training with a mixture of off-policy and on-policy data yielded the best verifier results, while only off-policy or only on-policy data performed worse.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotations were done by a subset of the authors.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: SWE-Bench's instance extraction script, SWE-Bench's versioning script, SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors state that they publicly release SWE-Gym, models, agent trajectories, pre-built Docker images for each instance, and open source all artifacts of the project including dataset, model weights, agent trajectory data, and the training pipeline.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that improving automated software engineering capabilities could increase developer productivity and accessibility across industries, support critical open-source infrastructure, and potentially make software development more accessible. It also notes that as these agents become more capable, they may impact software engineering jobs and require careful consideration around code ownership, licensing, and attribution. The authors further warn that similar techniques could potentially be misused to automate the creation of malicious code, and encourage future work on responsible deployment including security, safety, and economic impacts.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that task distribution across repositories exhibits a long-tail pattern, with pandas comprising nearly one-third of the total and bokeh about one percent. It also states that ignoring executable environments could introduce distribution bias, diminishing SWE-Gym's utility, which motivated manual environment configuration. In self-improvement experiments, the authors observe that repeated sampling introduces a bias toward easier tasks because task success probability follows a long-tail distribution, and they propose per-instance capping to mitigate this easy-task bias. The paper also notes that alternative concurrent work that discards instances failing setup may bias the environment away from tasks with complex dependencies.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper states that SWE-Gym is limited by environment diversity, including the number of repositories, types of tasks, and programming languages. It also notes that SWE-Gym tasks are on average harder than SWE-Bench tasks and that performance may be lower due to inclusion of sophisticated repositories like pandas and MONAI. The authors report that self-improvement results are modest and not yet working effectively in some settings. They also note that current SWE settings focus solely on task completion and neglect human-in-the-loop collaboration, and that current models are primarily research artifacts and not yet production-ready.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a training environment for software engineering agents and verifier models. The paper uses SWE-Gym to train language-model-based SWE agents, to train verifier or reward models on successful and unsuccessful agent trajectories, and to study training-time and inference-time scaling. SWE-Gym Lite is described as suitable for rapid prototyping. SWE-Gym Raw is released to support future research in SWE agent development and automatic dataset synthesis.
